channel.title: Tech Xplore - electronic gadgets, technology advances and research news
channel.description: Tech Xplore internet news portal provides the latest news on electronics, technology, and engineering.

item.title: Finding the catalyst sweet spot for turning CO₂ into methane
item.description: Capturing carbon dioxide is only one part of the climate challenge. Another question is what to do with the captured CO₂. One promising route is to convert CO₂ into useful fuels and chemicals, especially when the process can be paired with renewable hydrogen.

item.title: Researchers use data from 130 wells worldwide to speed up drilling-fluid solids checks
item.description: As the world faces ongoing pressure to secure reliable energy supplies while controlling costs and improving operational efficiency, even small delays in drilling operations can have significant consequences. For oil, gas and geothermal drilling, one of the routine but important checks is determining how much solid material is present in the drilling fluid.

item.title: After AI, EU bets on quantum as next big thing
item.description: Fearing Europe could lose ground in another technology race, as it lags behind the United States and China on AI, the European Union will unveil plans on Wednesday that it says will make the continent a global quantum computing powerhouse.

item.title: Fake gifts, real losses as AI ads proliferate
item.description: Online shoppers endlessly scrolling through gift suggestions this holiday season risk being duped by a blizzard of AI-generated scams touting nonexistent products.

item.title: An unclassified CIA system was breached in a cyberattack
item.description: An unclassified CIA system was breached in a cyberattack, according to a person familiar with the incident who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity.

item.title: Georgia Waffle House cuts cooling energy use by 40% with new salt-based AC system
item.description: In July 2025, a team of technicians walked into a Waffle House in Macon, Georgia. That month, peak temperatures hovered around 92 degrees Fahrenheit (33 degrees Celsius). In the restaurant's kitchen, where cooks fried patty melts, hash browns and waffles on an oil-slick grill, temperatures could feel just as hot, if not hotter.

item.title: Think you're anonymous online? AI can blow your cover
item.description: Doxxing—exposing someone's personal information, like a name or address—has long been a way to settle scores in internet feuds. But in the age of AI, a nightmare might simply start with a chatbot stepping out of line.

item.title: Greece's data center boom angers locals near Athens
item.description: As the sun sets in the semirural community of Spata near Athens, a group of pupils stretch on the sports field of Pierce College, one of Greece's top international schools.

item.title: Loom seamlessly combines weaving, knitting and braiding
item.description: Cornell researchers have developed a loom that seamlessly incorporates weaving, braiding and knitting-like techniques to create new kinds of textiles.

item.title: Space lasers are fast, but clouds still rule the forecast
item.description: Since the launch of Sputnik, humanity has talked to its spacecraft through radio waves. Radio is great for communication through any weather, but it has hit a limit—traditional radio frequencies are highly regulated by bodies like the International Telecommunications Union, which limits the scalability of radio communications networks to meet the growing demand for bandwidth to and from space. The obvious solution is to switch to infrared lasers, which have an extremely high data transfer rate.

item.title: Excess renewable energy could power new industrial processes
item.description: As the U.S. expands its reliance on renewable energy, a considerable amount of excess electricity will be generated by solar and wind power plants. A new study explores how this energy could potentially be harnessed by certain technologies or production processes, reducing costs and increasing energy efficiency.

item.title: 'Glosslighting' the public: Study calls for overhaul of industry-led AI buzzwords
item.description: Superintelligence? More like super-confusing. A Simon Fraser University study warns that industry-led AI jargon may be distorting public understanding of the technology and its harms.

item.title: Predicting the unknown: A robust approach lets AI extrapolate to undiscovered materials
item.description: Imagine asking a computer to predict the properties of a material it has never seen before. It may perform well when the new material resembles something in its training data, but its predictions can become unreliable when it encounters something truly unfamiliar. This poses a challenge for materials discovery, where suitable candidates often lie outside existing data. This is the problem of extrapolation, and researchers have now demonstrated a practical way to address it.

item.title: Thin lenses, clear images in bright daylight: A step toward everyday AR glasses
item.description: A new technology could make augmented reality (AR) glasses—which overlay information such as directions or text onto the scene in front of the wearer—more practical for everyday use. By reducing light loss inside a thin lens, a Korean research team has built prototype glasses that display legible text even in bright outdoor conditions.

item.title: New rewritable displays can show an image for months without power
item.description: Researchers from the ARC Center of Excellence for Transformative Meta-Optical Systems (TMOS) are the first to report a reflective display based on antimony selenide that can hold an image for months without being powered.

item.title: Trade war over green tech has no winners
item.description: In a study published in the journal Energy Research & Social Science, Dr. Lukas Hermwille and three co-authors outline the consequences of a trade war over environmental technologies. Such a trade war would significantly drive up the global costs of combating climate change—with Europe being hit hardest. There is reason to fear that this would make achieving the global climate targets difficult, if not impossible.

item.title: Chatbots may leapfrog web search in sub-Saharan Africa
item.description: AI chatbots may leapfrog web search in sub-Saharan Africa, according to a study of teachers in Sierra Leone. Mobile phones are common in Africa, but only 37% of the population uses the internet. Among those internet users, social networking apps are much more commonly used than search engines, in part because search brings up large foreign websites that gobble up costly data to download.

item.title: Smart homes of the future must put people before technology
item.description: Homes that automatically adjust their temperature, manage electricity use and monitor residents' well-being could transform everyday living in the future, but smarter technology does not necessarily mean better homes.

item.title: New laser welding process joins aluminum castings with fewer pores and less spatter
item.description: Laser welding can now join cast aluminum directly to cast aluminum. Producing high-quality joints between aluminum die-cast components has long been a major challenge. Process-related pores and gas inclusions in the material can open during conventional laser beam welding. The released gases cause pores in the weld and sometimes violent melt ejections, compromising joint quality.

item.title: UK 'Grand Theft Auto VI' hacker gets 7-year sentence
item.description: A U.K. court sentenced a British hacker to seven years in jail Monday for a series of cyberattacks, including leaking footage from "Grand Theft Auto VI" years before the blockbuster game's release.

item.title: Harnessing glacial lakes for hydropower
item.description: As mountain glaciers retreat in the face of a warming climate, glacial lakes are expanding, increasing the risk of glacial lake outburst flood events that cause damage and destruction to communities downstream. However, harnessing the power of this excess water could both provide a renewable energy source for these communities and help reduce flood risks.

item.title: Technology for 'printing' steel could help extend the life of aging bridges and buildings
item.description: The U.K. has an enormous amount of steel in service across critical infrastructure. Yet every day, millions of people cross bridges without giving much thought to the structures beneath their feet.

item.title: New benchmark could help AI keep up with current events
item.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is struggling to keep up with the world. When queried about recent events, chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude often rely on the same sources people have used for years to find information online.

item.title: Rwanda and Papua New Guinea had big energy access plans: Study compares what happened
item.description: In both Rwanda and Papua New Guinea, only about 10% of the population had electricity in the early 2000s. Both countries have rural populations that are difficult to reach with national electricity grids. Both partly privatized their electricity sectors and set ambitious targets for increased energy access.

item.title: 'Grand Theft Auto VI' lives up to its hype with compelling characters and spectacular action
item.description: "Grand Theft Auto VI" has gotten all kinds of attention since its release last week. It generated a record $3.79 billion in first-day retail sales. Workers around the world took personal days to dig into the franchise's first installment in 13 years. Tributes and parodies showed up everywhere from a Miami Heat game to the White House's social media feeds.

item.title: New synthetic graphite paves way for rapid EV charging
item.description: Lithium-ion batteries, like those found in cars, cell phones and cameras, often have anodes made of graphite. During charging, lithium ions move into the graphite anode. How quickly they can move through the graphite is one of the key factors limiting how fast a battery can charge. James Tour's lab at Rice University has recently developed a new kind of synthetic graphite, one that supports much faster charging and can be produced in a fraction of a second.

item.title: Thanksgiving travel could be messy with storms coming after a week filled with airline glitches
item.description: Traveling for the Thanksgiving holiday is shaping up to be a bit chaotic, following a cascade of glitches that have upended airlines the past weeks, the threat of storms on both coasts and soaring airfares.

item.title: European Commission warns EU Academy users of data leak after AI-driven cyberattack
item.description: The European Commission on Monday warned users of one of its websites that personal data has been leaked in a major AI-generated cyberattack that was launched on the EU institution last month.

item.title: Bubbles to the rescue: Scientists make nuclear reactors better, one tiny sphere at a time
item.description: Tiny helium bubbles injected into the liquid fuel of advanced nuclear reactors are supposed to clean out radioactive materials. But nuclear scientists in the 1960s and 1970s learned that there is a limit to their cleaning power. Similar to soap scum building up in a bathtub, the bubbles clean—until they don't.

item.title: CrowdStrike to acquire Zscaler in a $44 billion deal that would create a cybersecurity giant
item.description: CrowdStrike is buying cloud security company Zscaler in an all-stock deal worth about $43.9 billion, the companies said Monday, in a major acquisition that combines two of the cybersecurity industry's biggest names.
